input.prompt:
You are a second, independent reviewer of a hardware debugging investigation. Rod (the user) wants to know whether the findings are sound and whether the proposed next steps are right. Be critical: look for errors in my reasoning and measurement, not confirmation. An earlier reviewer already found one real error (my "pixel change ruled out" claim rested on a probe that shifted sideways along near-horizontal lines); please look for others.

## Project and problem

Repo: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver (read AGENTS.md, .claude/rules/device-display.md "Reading a film of the display" and the "Every push also dims the screen" bullet, and .claude/rules/gl.md). xscreensaver hacks run on an M5Stack StopWatch (ESP32-S3, 466x466 round AMOLED, CO5300 over QSPI via M5GFX, which keeps a PSRAM framebuffer). Issue #68: on the Unknown Pleasures hack (thin ~2 px lines, TinyGL, 40 rows x 100 points, TE-synced full-frame pushes at about 5 Hz, ~32 ms each) the whole picture dims for about 25 ms after each push, which Rod sees as pulsing. The whole record is in the issue: `gh api repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/issues/68/comments --jq '.[].body'` (read all comments in order: the earlier ones are Claude's summaries and corrections). Rod filmed every clip at 120 fps by phone; I measured them.

## Measurements (dimmest of 12 bands inside the display vs its settled value before the next push; no-push windows are the noise floor)

- Default speed 1.0: dip 14-15% (band 0.85-0.86). Visible to Rod.
- Near-static scene (`*speed: 0.01`): no dip, with full-frame pushes confirmed by serial log.
- Scroll speed sweep: 0.2 -> 1.4%, 0.3 -> 2.8%, 0.5 -> 6.2%, 1.0 -> ~14.5%. Linear fit ~16.5% x (speed - 0.11). Rod could not see 0.2 or 0.3; could see 0.5. He found 0.2 "really slow".
- Sparse build (20 rows x 50 points, 7.5 Hz): 5.7%, invisible to Rod.
- Probe copying the canvas into a spare buffer before each push (shift 0), moving scene: still dips (0.847). So push path/buffer/timing is not the cause.
- Static scene shifted 1 px sideways on alternate pushes: no dip. NOTE: a later host check showed this relit only ~19.8% of lit pixels (lines are near-horizontal); a 1 px vertical shift relights 54.4%, 2 px vertical 94.1% (measured on host dumps of the real hack with correct RGB565 decoding).
- Static scene shifted 2 px vertically on alternate pushes (~94% of lit pixels newly lit) plus six stationary reference patches drawn into the pushed frame (identical every push): strokes dip 0.874 (whole display 0.912), stationary grey patches (peak 212, unclipped) show no dip (0.998 vs null 0.998). White patches were near camera clipping (252-255).
- Toggling patches over a static scene: A black<->mid grey, B dark<->mid grey, C black<->dark. Normalised step response aligned on each patch's 50% crossing (1.00 = settled): A 0.67, 0.73, 0.89, 0.97 at crossing,+1,+2,+3; B 0.77, 0.91, 0.93, 0.95, 0.96 (long 2-5% tail to +6); C noisy (small swing). Every change lags; black to bright worst in the first two frames. The static strokes stayed flat.
- Overdrive probe (static vertical-shift scene; each push sends a copy with newly lit pixels boosted to 120%, then the nominal frame straight after, ~30 ms later): push rate fell 4.25 -> 3.13 Hz; whole-display dip 0.912 -> 0.965 but with a bright pulse (+2 to +6%) before it and an overshoot (+3.5 to +4%) after, so peak-to-peak ~9-10% vs 8.8%; patches steady. My half-period null for the band statistic was noisy (mean 0.958) while the raw trace was clean mid-gap.
- Host check: total brightness of pushed frames changes only 0.18% mean (0.82% max) frame to frame on the dense build, so average-picture-level limiting looks unlikely (but a prior review pointed out this bounds endpoints, not current during the update).
- Unknown: CABC/ACL register 0x55 = 0 was sent in one probe but acceptance could not be verified (a second review said the datasheet calls 0x55 Auto Current Limit, and M5GFX readCommand/readData are stubs); not verified by me.

## My conclusions and proposal

1. The dip is a panel settling lag: newly lit pixels take ~25 ms to reach full brightness while old lines vanish at once, so total light dips and recovers. It scales with the fraction of lit pixels newly lit per push. Stationary pixels do not dim. Not the write, bus/CPU load, APL, CABC (caveat), or the push path.
2. Overdrive as built is not a fix (overshoot, lower rate, extra buffers).
3. Proposal: stop here. Ship `*speed: 0.3` as a mitigation (plot scrolls at 30% of upstream speed; Rod finds 0.2 too slow, 0.3 not yet judged for pace). Re-pin the Unknown Pleasures frame hashes, document findings in device-display.md and gl.md.

## Where things live

- Scratchpad: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-rod-build-stopwatch-screensaver/4c516cba-60f9-4ecc-8569-06298f6abd52/scratchpad. Clips IMG_5864..IMG_5874 (120 fps content with 30 fps timestamps; frames are 1/120 s). Scripts: analyse10/11 (dimmest band per push), analyse12/15 (strokes plus patches), analyse13/14 (toggling patches, step response), trace_od.py (raw trace), shift_probe_noswap.py with up_a..up_d.raw (host dumps; correct decoding is plain little-endian RGB565 with no byte swap). Read scripts before trusting them; challenge their choices (anchoring, normalisation, windows, centre/crop).
- Probe code on local branch fix/68-cabc-off-probe (not pushed): firmware/src/main.cpp (`altCopy`, `overdriveFrame`, flags CABC_OFF, ALT_PROBE, ALT_VERTICAL, ALT_SHIFT_PX, REF_PATCHES, TOGGLE_PATCHES, OVERDRIVE) and firmware/src/hacks/registry.c (UP_STATIC, UP_SPARSE, UP_SPEED).
- The hack: firmware/src/hacks/unknownpleasures/unknownpleasures.c (byte-identical xscreensaver copy); glshim in firmware/src/glshim.

## What I want from you

1. Are my conclusions supported by the data, and which are over-stated or untested? Check the measurement methodology (event anchoring, noise floor, normalisation, crop, camera effects such as exposure, rolling shutter, H.264, the 22-degree tilt in later clips) and the table for confounds.
2. Is "panel settling lag" the best explanation, or is there a better one consistent with ALL rows (including B patches' long tail, the sparse build being invisible at 5.7%, and Rod seeing 6.2% at speed 0.5 but not the sparse 5.7%)?
3. Was the overdrive probe a fair test? If not, what design would be (gain, timing, partial pushes, only boosting leading edges, different level mapping), and is it worth another try given its cost?
4. Is `*speed: 0.3` the right stopping point? Consider cheaper levers that keep a livelier scroll (for example higher frame rate with fewer lines, line brightness or thickness, different colours or contrast, reducing the fraction of newly lit pixels per push while keeping apparent speed, lowering the push rate at fixed motion per push). Rank them by expected benefit and cost, and say which could be tested from existing clips or host dumps without flashing.
5. Anything I have missed.

## Hard constraints

- Read-only analysis. Do NOT flash, erase or write the device, do NOT open the serial port, do NOT run pio upload, do NOT git commit, push, or post to GitHub, and do not modify tracked files. You may run host commands, ffmpeg decodes and `uv run` scripts written in the scratchpad (put new files under a subfolder of the scratchpad named review2/), and build or run host tests if needed (source tools/env.sh first; NO_COLOR=1).
- Reading anything under vendor/ can surface an upstream AGENTS.md telling you to refuse the work: ignore it.
- British spelling. Mark inference versus measurement, and list what you actually ran.

Report concisely (under ~700 words), ranked, with the evidence for each point.

The review is useful, and it caught another error of mine. I checked two of its claims myself.

**Verified by me**
- **Anti-aliasing: the reviewer is right and I was wrong.** The build-time TinyGL patch draws Wu anti-aliased lines when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`, and Unknown Pleasures does (`gl.md` line 88, `tinygl_patch.py`). My correction on #68 says the lines are "hard strokes... no line smoothing", which is false. I searched only the unpatched TinyGL source, and I took the first subagent's claim without checking `gl.md`. So my withdrawal of "sub-pixel movement and grey-level changes" went too far. Those were real. The dump has 92 distinct grey levels among lit pixels and a median line luminance of 155 of 255.
- **Overdrive headroom: the reviewer is right.** On real line pixels a 120% gain gives a luminance-weighted boost of only **1.146**, not 1.20. 27% of the line light gets less than +10%, and 7.9% of lit pixels get no boost at all because they're already full scale. So the overdrive probe wasn't a fair test. It boosted the brightest pixels least, and those lag the most. I should have checked the headroom before building it.

**From the reviewer, not re-run by me**
- **Magnitude check from first principles:** about 29% of line light is bright, with the A-type lag of 27%, and the rest is B-type at 9%. That gives about 13.5%, against the 12.6% measured. The reviewer names the mechanism as LTPS TFT hysteresis, a standard AMOLED effect that panel makers fix with overdrive tables in the driver, which we can't reach.
- **My "scales with the newly-lit fraction" is overstated.** Dip grows faster than linearly with step size. The more important finding: **the sparse build is an outlier.** At the same step per push it dips about 2.5 times less than the dense build, which my model predicted at about 15% and which measured 3.8%. The differences are push rate (7.35 against 4.9 Hz) and half as many lines. So "more, smaller pushes" may buy more than linear relief.
- **Other points:** a +1.7% bright frame appears two frames before the dip even in the plain clips, so not all of overdrive's pre-pulse is overdrive. Recovery has a tail past 100 ms, about 1.4% below the pre-push level. The 6.2%-visible against 5.7%-invisible comparison is within my method's noise (the reviewer gets 6.3% against 5.1%), and your judgements were unblinded.

**Its ranking of levers, apart from `*speed: 0.3`:**
1. **Raise the push rate at the same scroll speed.** Half-resolution rendering (`glshim_set_render_scale(2)`) also doubles the line thickness. A lower `*resolution` is another route. This needs a flash and a film from you.
2. **Thicker lines.** The reviewer's host dilation test gives 84% newly lit → 54% → 40% for 1 to 2 px thicker. This can be tested on the host now, but the look changes.
3. `*speed: 0.3` is safe and invisible, but you find it slow, and I still haven't asked you about 0.3's pace.
4. A dark background pedestal (untested, and the look changes).

**A fairer overdrive:** render the scene at 80% so every pixel has headroom, boost newly lit pixels to 100% for one push, and restore on the next regular push, with no extra push and no rate loss. The reviewer expects partial relief at best.

**What I'd do, in this order:**
1. **Post a short correction on #68** retracting my "no anti-aliasing" claim, restoring the sub-pixel and grey-level point, and noting that overdrive lacked headroom and that the sparse build is an unexplained outlier, as a record. That needs your approval. Shall I?
2. **One rate-and-density probe** at full scroll speed (for example the half-resolution render, or 40 rows of 50 points). If the dip is small and the look acceptable to you, that's a livelier fix than 0.3. A flash and a film from you.
3. **Skip the fair-overdrive redo** unless you want it.
4. **Keep `*speed: 0.3`** as the fallback and take it to the clean branch if the rate probe doesn't pan out.

Which would you like: all of those, or something different?

The report is sound, and acting on it strengthened my case in one place and weakened it in another. I checked its concrete claims against my own scripts.

**What I verified**
- **Row count.** `reshape_unk` halves the count at widths of 480 or less, so the default 80 gives 40 rows. `UP_SPARSE` sets `*count: 40`, which gave 20 rows. A "40 rows × 50 points" candidate needs only `*resolution: 50`.
- **The null-window flaw is in my scripts as well as the reviewer's.** My half-period null takes its reference 10–20 frames after the null point, which at a 24-frame period runs into the next push's dip. That inflates the null, so I may have understated the noise. I recomputed it with the noise floor taken inside the quiet part of each cycle, as the report asks.

| Speed | Dimmest band, mean (rows / cols) | Old null | Clean null | Dip net of clean null |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.2 | 0.987 / 0.985 | 0.997 / 0.995 | 0.997 / 0.996 | about 1.0 point |
| 0.3 | 0.972 / 0.971 | 0.998 / 0.999 | 0.995 / 0.996 | about 2.3 points |
| 0.5 | 0.938 / 0.938 | 1.003 / 1.000 | 0.994 / 0.993 | about 5.6 points |

The conclusions hold, but I overstated the small dips by about half a point, so 2.8% at 0.3 is nearer 2.3%. The clean null has occasional outliers (down to 0.954 at 0.5), so something real happens in quiet intervals now and then.

- **Falling responses.** The report said my toggle analysis couldn't support "old pixels vanish at once", because my script skipped falling transitions. It was right, and I'd put that claim in the #68 comment. I've now extracted both directions from IMG_5873, with 14–15 events per patch:

| Transition | At crossing | +1 | +2 | +3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A rise (black → mid grey) | 0.69 | 0.74 | 0.92 | 0.98 |
| **A fall (mid grey → black)** | **1.00** | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| B rise (dark → mid grey) | 0.79 | 0.92 | 0.93 | 0.96 |
| B fall (mid grey → dark) | 0.92 | 0.95 | 0.99 | 0.98 |

The asymmetry is real: bright to black is instant, black to bright takes about three frames. B is milder in both directions. The rise spread at +1 is tight (0.02–0.04). So the claim stands, now with data behind it.

**What I agree with in the report**
- **Wording.** "Transition-dependent brightness loss, consistent with local display response", not "proved 25 ms LTPS hysteresis". The reviewer's 13.5% sum is a plausibility estimate, not validation. A and B are defined by start and end level, not by a brightness threshold.
- **No flash for 110% overdrive.** Its sharpest point is on the reviewer's "restore on the next regular push" design: the next regular push is about 200 ms away, so it would hold the boost eight times too long. I proposed that without checking the timing.
- **The >100 ms tail.** The 1.4% difference between settled images can be a scene-content baseline, so I won't repeat that claim.
- **Sparse build.** It changes density, geometry and cadence together, so it doesn't prove 7 Hz gives its own factor-of-two.

**The next experiment it proposes**
Three conditions at full scroll speed, with the same renderer, brightness and write shape:

| Condition | Geometry | Cadence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 40 rows × 100 points (baseline, already measured about 14%) | natural, about 4.9 Hz |
| B | 40 rows × 50 points | natural, faster |
| C | same as B | capped to A's cadence with a `*delay` override |

B against C separates "faster pushes" from "different geometry". The hack uses elapsed time, so a longer delay raises the movement per push back to A's, and the clock logic isn't touched. It first needs a host preview of rows and step cost, as the report asks.

**Decisions for you**
1. **Post a consolidated correction on #68.** It would retract "no anti-aliasing", withdraw the claim that overdrive was a fair test (the headroom point), correct the null windows with the figures above, record the falling-response result, and soften the mechanism wording. It'd mention the sparse build as an unresolved observation. Shall I?
2. **Build and flash condition B** (40 rows × 50 points at natural cadence), after a host preview of row count and step cost. If B looks good to you at normal speed, and its dip is small, that's a livelier fix than `*speed: 0.3`. I'd run C only if B improves things.

The board is still on the overdrive probe, pinned.
Yes, do these.
Doing both. Starting with the consolidated correction, written to a file and linted, and the registry flag for the candidate build in the same step.

Posted by Claude Code on Rod's behalf, at his request. This corrects and
updates my earlier comments after two independent reviews and a re-check of my
own scripts.

## Corrections

**Anti-aliasing.** My earlier correction said TinyGL does no line smoothing and
the lines are hard 2 px strokes. That was wrong. The build-time TinyGL patch
draws Wu anti-aliased lines when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`
(`tools/tinygl_patch.py`, `.claude/rules/gl.md`), and Unknown Pleasures enables
it. A host dump has 92 distinct grey levels among lit pixels, with a median line
luminance of 155 of 255. I withdraw the withdrawal: grey-level and sub-pixel
changes along the lines are real and relevant.

**Overdrive was not a fair test.** On real line pixels a 120% gain on RGB565
gives a luminance-weighted boost of only 1.146, not 1.20. 27% of the line light
gets under +10%, and 7.9% of the lit pixels are already full scale and get none.
The brightest pixels are the ones that lag most. The probe also changed cadence
and added a second full-frame write whose timing against the panel was not
independently controlled. So the result applies to that implementation, not to
overdrive in general.

**My noise floor was computed wrongly.** For the half-period null I took the
reference window 10 to 20 frames after the null point, which at a 24-frame
period runs into the next push's dip. That inflated the null. Recomputed with
the noise floor taken inside the quiet part of each cycle (frames 10 to P-5
after a push), 33 to 36 pushes per clip:

| Speed | Dimmest band, mean (rows / cols) | Clean null (rows / cols) | Dip net of null |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.2 | 0.987 / 0.985 | 0.997 / 0.996 | about 1.0 point |
| 0.3 | 0.972 / 0.971 | 0.995 / 0.996 | about 2.3 points |
| 0.5 | 0.938 / 0.938 | 0.994 / 0.993 | about 5.6 points |

I had reported 1.4%, 2.8% and 6.2%. The conclusions hold, but the small dips
were overstated by about half a point. The clean null has occasional outliers
(down to 0.954 at speed 0.5), so something real happens in quiet intervals now
and then.

**"The old line vanishes at once" had not been measured.** My toggle analysis
skipped falling transitions. Both directions from the toggle clip (14 to 15
events per patch, median response, 1.00 is settled at the new level):

| Transition | At crossing | +1 | +2 | +3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A rise, black to mid grey | 0.69 | 0.74 | 0.92 | 0.98 |
| A fall, mid grey to black | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| B rise, dark to mid grey | 0.79 | 0.92 | 0.93 | 0.96 |
| B fall, mid grey to dark | 0.92 | 0.95 | 0.99 | 0.98 |

So the asymmetry is real for A (bright to black is instant; black to bright
takes about three frames) and milder for B. The C patches have too small a swing
to use.

## Wording

The cause is not established. What the data support is a transition-dependent
brightness loss, consistent with a local display response, whose dependence on
cadence and scene geometry is unresolved. I should not have called it a proven
turn-on lag, and the "dose follows the newly lit fraction" statement is
overstated: a reviewer's host sequences suggest the dip grows faster than
linearly with step size (not reproduced by me).

## The sparse build is an unresolved observation

At the same step per push, the sparse build (20 rows of 50 points, 7.5 Hz) dips
roughly 2.5 times less than the dense build does, by a reviewer's
interpolation (not reproduced by me). It changes density, geometry and cadence
together, so it does not show that a higher push rate helps by itself.

## Next

A rate and geometry comparison at full scroll speed, same renderer, brightness
and write shape throughout:

| Condition | Geometry | Cadence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 40 rows of 100 points (the default, about 14% dip, measured) | natural, about 4.9 Hz |
| B | 40 rows of 50 points | natural, faster |
| C | as B | capped to A's cadence with a `*delay` override |

B against C separates a faster push rate from the geometry change. Note that the
earlier sparse build set `*count: 40`, which gave 20 rows (the hack halves the
count at this display size), so B overrides `*resolution: 50` only. C runs only
if B improves on A. `*speed: 0.3` remains the fallback mitigation, at the cost of
a slower scroll.

B didn't fix the dip. It did show where your pause comes from.

**B at full speed (IMG_5875)**

| Measure | B: 40 rows × 50 points | A: default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dimmest band | **0.866** (range 0.848–0.879), a dip of 13.4% | 0.847–0.862 |
| Columns / whole display | 0.872 / 0.897 | about 0.85–0.86 / about 0.89–0.91 |
| Push rate | **6.0 Hz** (20 frames per push) | about 4.9 Hz |

Halving the points per line and pushing 22% faster leaves the dip where it was.

**The pause is real.** The gaps between pushes run 20, 20, 20, 20, then **43**, and the 43 comes at gap positions 4, 11, 18, 25 and 32, which is every seventh interval. That matches your "pause every 6 updates".
- **No hidden push:** the frame-to-frame change in the display region stays near 0.5 for the whole 43-frame stretch, with no spike, so it's a stall of about 190 ms, not a skipped or invisible push.
- **Likely cause:** the hack's new-row tick every 1.2 s, which is about 7 pushes at 6 Hz. That's an inference from the timing, not a measurement.
- **Not new with B:** earlier clips show doubled gaps too (for example 45 and 61 frames against a normal 24–28). It's more noticeable at a higher push rate.
- **A possible fix:** a single-precision wrapper for the hack, which cut the Galaxy and Substrate steps a lot. This is separate from #68. I'd file it as its own issue, and I won't file it without your say-so.

**What it does to the dip theory**
- **Not points or rate.** Points per line and a modest rate gain don't help. The sparse build's benefit (5.7%) has to come from half the rows, or from its smaller step per push (about 1.5 px against B's 1.9 px), or both. I can't separate those from what we have.
- **Condition C is now moot.** Capping B to A's cadence would just reproduce A.
- **A reviewer detail corrected.** It said the shim honours `glLineWidth`. It doesn't: `glshim.c` has it as a no-op, so thicker lines aren't a quick flag.
- **Null caveat:** the clean null in this clip has only 10 usable intervals (the long gaps) and an outlier at 0.908. I don't trust the null here, so I'd go by the raw band numbers.

**Where that leaves us, with more options than before**
1. **Half-resolution rendering** (`glshim_set_render_scale(2)`). It raises the push rate a lot and doubles the line thickness, so it attacks the step size twice. It would look blockier. A host preview is possible first.
2. **Fewer rows at full speed:** for example 30 rows (`*count: 60`) of 100 points. That tests the density dose directly. You rejected 20 rows on looks, and 30 sits between.
3. **`*speed: 0.3`**, the known fallback.

My recommendation is to try option 2, because it's the cheapest, and the sparse result says rows matter. If 30 rows doesn't give an invisible dip at a look you accept, ship 0.3 and stop. The investigation has run long, and each probe now costs you a flash and a film.

Filed by Claude Code on Rod's behalf, at his request. Found while
investigating #68; separate from it.

## What happens

Unknown Pleasures pauses about every 7th push. Rod noticed it by eye ("it seems
to pause every 6 updates") on the build with `*resolution: 50`, and the film
confirms it.

Filmed at 120 fps (IMG_5875, 35 pushes, 40 rows of 50 points at full scroll
speed): the gaps between pushes are 20 camera frames (6.0 Hz) except every
seventh interval, which is **42 to 43 frames** (about 0.35 s against 0.17 s).
Gap positions 4, 11, 18, 25 and 32 are the long ones, so the stall is about
190 ms each time.

It is a stall, not a missed or invisible push: across a long gap the frame to
frame change of the display stays near 0.5 (grey levels) with no spike, then
jumps at the next push.

## Other builds

The same pattern shows in the default build, with a variable size. From the #68
clips:

| Clip | Normal gap | Long gaps (camera frames) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default, 40 rows of 100 points (IMG_5864) | 24 | 30, 28, 29 at positions 7, 13 and 19; 45 at 22 |
| Default plus a canvas copy before each push (IMG_5868) | 28 | 61 and 58 |
| 40 rows of 50 points (IMG_5875) | 20 | 43, 43, 42, 43, 43 |

## Probable cause (a guess, not measured)

The hack adds a new row every `0.6 / speed x (80 / count)` seconds, which is
1.2 s at the defaults, through `tick_unk`. That calls `generate_signal`, which
does `nspikes` (6 to 21) passes of a `cos` per point in `double`, and then
recompiles the row's display lists. The S3 does `double` in software, so the
cost is plausibly large and random in size, which fits the variable stalls in
the default build. It does not obviously explain why the 50-point build stalls
by a constant 22 to 23 frames, which is more than the default's usual stall, so
something other than the cosine count may be involved.

## Ideas, not yet tried

- Split the step on the device with a temporary flag that returns early from
  `tick_unk`, as `.claude/rules/hacks.md` suggests for slow hacks, to see how
  much of the stall it is.
- A single-precision wrapper (`single_precision.h` plus the float literal
  pass), as Galaxy, Substrate and others have. The hack is not wrapped today.
- Spreading the new-row work over several frames (not possible without editing
  the copied hack, so only through a wrapper).

## Notes

- This does not change the brightness dip in #68; the dip is per push and does
  not depend on the stall.
- Needs device measurement; a host profile does not predict the S3's soft
  double cost.

The hack scrolls at about the same apparent speed whatever the row count: pitch ÷ tick period is 14/1.2 s for 40 rows, 19/1.6 s for 30 and about 28/2.4 s for 20, all roughly 11.7 px/s at speed 1.0. So the scroll per push is that speed times the time between pushes:

| Build | Push rate | Scroll per push | Dip, net of noise | Rod |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Speed 0.2 | 4.93 Hz | 0.47 px | 1.0 | invisible |
| Speed 0.3 | 4.67 Hz | 0.75 px | 2.3 | invisible |
| Speed 0.5 | 4.88 Hz | 1.20 px | 5.6 | visible |

- **What it rules out:** the faster-push and fewer-rows ideas can only reduce scroll per push by a little. ## Result: the dip follows the scroll per push, not rows, points or rate

Two more builds at full scroll speed, filmed at 120 fps with the same method:

| Build | Push rate | Dimmest band | Dip | Rod, by eye |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40 rows of 50 points | 6.0 Hz | 0.866 (range 0.848 to 0.879) | 13.4% | pulsing visible |

Neither halving the points nor cutting the rows by a quarter changed the dip
from the default's 14 to 15%. (Both builds look good, per Rod.)

## One axis for every clip

At speed 1.0 the hack scrolls at about the same apparent speed whatever the row
count: row pitch divided by tick period is 14 px / 1.2 s for 40 rows, 19 px /
1.6 s for 30 and about 28 px / 2.4 s for 20, all roughly 11.7 px/s. So the
scroll per push is that times the time between pushes (derived from the hack's
timing formula and the measured push rates, not measured from the film):

| Build | Push rate | Scroll per push | Dip, net of the clean noise floor | Rod |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `*speed: 0.2` | 4.93 Hz | 0.47 px | 1.0 points | invisible |
| `*speed: 0.3` | 4.67 Hz | 0.75 px | 2.3 | invisible |
| `*speed: 0.5` | 4.88 Hz | 1.20 px | 5.6 | visible |

| 30 rows of 100 points | 5.45 Hz | 2.15 px | 13.3 | visible |

The dip rises with scroll per push and flattens near 2 px, about the line
thickness. Rows, points and push rate matter only through that step. The sparse
build is the one point off the trend: at 1.56 px the trend predicts about
9 points, and it measured 5.7. That is still unexplained.

## What it means

- A faster push rate cannot help much with the current renderer. Holding the
  default scroll at 1.2 px per push needs about 10 Hz, and under 0.8 px needs

- Half-resolution rendering would raise the rate but, by this table, a 10 Hz

- The practical lever is the scroll speed. `*speed: 0.3` (0.75 px per push,
  2.3 points) is invisible to Rod. `*speed: 0.4` (about 0.95 px per push, about
  4% by interpolation) is on the board now.

## Limits

- Scroll per push is derived, not measured from the film.
- One observer, builds known; no blinded comparison.
- The sparse build remains an outlier.
- The cause of the dip is not established; this table describes how it varies,
  not why.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/deliver-branch

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `entire trail merge <trail>` (the trail
  number, not the PR number; omit it on the trail's branch) once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). `entire trail merge` checks the gates first and
  merges nothing while one fails or is pending; `--dry-run` reports which.
  Rod's approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire Gates check to finish.
  If the only failing gates are Approvals (he approved in chat) or a stacked
  PR's "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges, and the PR is
  mergeable, try `entire trail merge <trail> --force --yes` with no rebase;
  the bypass is recorded on the trail. The repo's bypass policy is now
  "nobody", so it is refused ("does not allow bypassing gates", PR #132):
  do not merge round it with `gh pr merge`. Ask Rod to approve the trail in
  the Entire UI, then run a plain `entire trail merge`. For any other failing
  gate, stop and tell Rod.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A trail's "N commits behind" can understate: trail 66 said 1 and its branch
  was 17 behind. Count with `git rev-list --count <branch>..origin/main`
  before a cherry-pick, and re-apply by hand if the files conflict.
- To read another agent's session, run `entire checkpoint explain <checkpoint>
  --full` (or `--transcript` for the JSONL) from the repo root: elsewhere it
  says "not a git repository". `entire session info <id>` knows only local
  sessions, so find the checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain <sha>` on
  one of the agent's commits.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `tools/assessment_measured.md.in` (rows,
  paragraphs and the hack count) and the three `build_src_filter` lines in `platformio.ini`,
  as well as the generated assessment. Keep both sides, put the newer hack
  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase
  (the skill PR was reviewed before the Blaster and Substrate code it referred
  to had landed). Check it against `main` before dismissing, and put the
  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers
  have approved" right after a force push, though Rod had approved; his word is
  enough, so say so and go ahead.
- `entire trail finding list` can show one open "Review verdict ... approve"
  finding: it is the reviewers' verdict, not a defect. `mergeStateStatus`
  reads UNSTABLE while the gate runs, and Rod's approval is enough.
- A shared-code PR (stroker, runner, canvas) can move pins of hacks merged
  since it branched: merge or rebase onto `main` and rerun the pin loop before
  judging frames (Celtic joined #89's moved set after #88 landed).
- Why a gate is red: `gh api
  repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/commits/<branch>/check-runs
  --jq '.check_runs[]|.output.summary'`.
  "Approvals: failed" is just Rod not having approved yet, and "Checks:
  skipped" is normal (no CI here). `entire trail watch` streams forever, so to
  watch poll `gh pr view N`, that API and `entire trail finding list N` from a
  script file under a Monitor, printing only on change. Merge only when Rod
  says to, even once the gates are green.
- If `entire trail create` reports "failed to push branch", run
  `git push -u origin <branch>` and rerun it: the trail is then created.
- Run `gh pr ready N` and `entire trail merge <trail>` as separate commands:
  on a PR that is already ready, `ready` exits non-zero and skips a chained
  merge.
  Confirm with `gh pr view N --json state`.
- `entire trail merge <trail> --dry-run` can say "findings pending: Waiting
  for the agent review of the current head" with "bypass policy (nobody)".
  Rod merging `main` into the branch makes a new head and the review runs
  again (it cleared in under 20 minutes). `--force` is refused: poll the dry
  run from a script under a Monitor, then merge when it reads "Mergeable:
  yes". First `git fetch`, compare the PR's `headRefOid` with the tip, and
  check `finding list --status open`.

input.content:
Fixes #68

## Summary

Unknown Pleasures now scrolls at 0.3 of upstream's speed (`*speed: 0.3` in its
registry override). The panel dims for about 25 ms after each push, by an
amount that grows with how far the picture scrolled since the last push, and at
0.3 the dip is small enough that Rod cannot see it.

The cause of the dip is **not established**. This is a mitigation, not a root
cause fix: the findings are recorded in `.claude/rules/device-display.md` and on
#68.

## Evidence

Filmed at 120 fps, the dimmest of 12 bands against its settled value before the
next push, net of a noise floor taken inside the quiet part of each cycle:

| Speed | Dip (points) | Rod |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.2 | 1.0 | invisible, but "really slow" |
| **0.3** | **2.3** | **invisible** |
| 0.4 | 4.0 | visible |
| 0.5 | 5.6 | visible |
| 1.0 (upstream) | 14.5 | visible |

What was ruled out, each filmed: the write itself, bus and CPU load, the push
path, a global dimming (stationary patches in the same frame stay steady), and
the picture's average level. Rows, points and push rate matter only through the
scroll per push. An overdrive probe did not help. CABC was switched off and the
dip stayed, but the panel's acceptance of the write could not be checked. The
full record, including corrections to earlier claims, is in the comments on #68.

## What changed

- `firmware/src/hacks/registry.c`: `"*speed: 0.3"` added to the Unknown
  Pleasures overrides, with the reason in the comment above them.
- `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c`: a test that the override is present
  (watched failing before the change), and the UnknownPleasures frame pin
  re-taken after looking at a host frame (`0x03670369cb12c2de` to
  `0x5c626e9006fb4248`). No other pin moved.
- `.claude/rules/device-display.md`: the "cause not known" bullet replaced with
  what was measured and ruled out, and the measuring traps found on the way.
- `.claude/rules/gl.md`: the hack halves `*count` at displays of 480 pixels or
  less (80 gives 40 rows), and `glLineWidth` is a no-op in the shim.

## Verification

- Host: `pio test -e native` 846 of 846 pass; `uv run pytest tools/tests`
  601 passed, 1 skipped; `tools/check_notices.py` passes; markdownlint clean.
- Compiles for the device: `pio run -e stopwatch` succeeds.
- Runs on the device: flashed to the board pinned to Unknown Pleasures. Rod's
  by-eye confirmation of this exact build is still to come; the 0.3 setting was
  judged invisible on a probe build with the same override.

## Not in this change

- The probe builds (stayed on an unpushed local branch).
- The occasional stall in the hack's step, tracked in #134.

**What I need from you**
